questions.q: In his 1845 Narrative, Douglass said he learned to read partly by trading what with poor white boys on Baltimore's streets?
questions.explain: Douglass wrote that he gave hungry white boys bread in exchange for reading lessons after Hugh Auld forbade his wife to keep teaching him.

questions.q: In 1851 Douglass merged The North Star with Gerrit Smith's Liberty Party Paper. What did he name the combined newspaper?
questions.explain: Frederick Douglass' Paper ran from 1851 until about 1860, after the merger with the Liberty Party Paper backed by abolitionist Gerrit Smith.

questions.q: In 1870 Douglass became editor and then owner of which Washington, D.C., weekly aimed at Black readers?
questions.explain: Douglass took over the New National Era in 1870 and kept it going until 1874, using it to press for civil rights during Reconstruction.

questions.q: Douglass's most often repeated lecture, first given in 1859 and delivered for decades, praised people who rose by their own effort. What was its title?
questions.explain: Douglass gave 'Self-Made Men' dozens of times; Acres of Diamonds was Russell Conwell's lecture and The Strenuous Life was Theodore Roosevelt's.

questions.q: Douglass's novella The Heroic Slave (1853) fictionalized Madison Washington, who led an 1841 revolt aboard which ship?
questions.explain: In 1841 enslaved people aboard the Creole seized the ship and sailed to the Bahamas, where most went free; it was Douglass's only work of fiction.

questions.q: Cedar Hill overlooks a neighborhood first laid out in 1854 as one of Washington's early suburbs. What was it originally called?
questions.explain: Uniontown was planned in 1854 across the Anacostia River for workers at the Navy Yard; the area later took the name Anacostia.

questions.q: In 1867 the Freedmen's Bureau bought land near Cedar Hill and sold lots to freedpeople, who built homes there. What was the settlement called?
questions.explain: Barry Farm in Anacostia was bought by the Freedmen’s Bureau; families paid for lots and built their own houses.

questions.q: The name Anacostia comes from the Algonquian-speaking people living along the river when John Smith explored the Potomac in 1608. Who were they?
questions.explain: John Smith recorded the Nacotchtank town near the river; the name, later Latinized as Anacostia, stayed on the river and the neighborhood.

questions.q: When Douglass escaped from Baltimore in September 1838, he rode north on a train of which line?
options: The Philadelphia, Wilmington and Baltimore Railroad
questions.explain: Carrying a free Black sailor's papers, Douglass boarded a northbound train of the Philadelphia, Wilmington and Baltimore line, then went on by ferry, steamboat and train.

questions.q: On his 1845 tour of Ireland, Douglass heard which Irish leader, an outspoken critic of American slavery, speak at a Dublin meeting?
questions.explain: Daniel O'Connell, the 'Liberator' who won Catholic emancipation, denounced American slavery; Douglass heard him speak in Dublin in 1845.

questions.q: What skilled trade did Douglass learn in Baltimore's shipyards before his escape?
questions.explain: Douglass worked as a caulker, sealing ship seams; his owner kept his wages, and in New Bedford white caulkers' prejudice kept him out of the trade.

questions.q: In 1879 Douglass surprised many by taking what stand on the Exoduster migration of Black Southerners to Kansas?
options: He raised money to charter trains to carry them to Kansas
He urged them to settle in Liberia instead of Kansas
He urged them to stay in the South and claim their rights there
He asked Congress to give them free western homesteads
questions.explain: Douglass argued that leaving the South gave up Black political power there; Richard Greener and others defended the Exodus.

questions.q: Which African American lieutenant governor served as acting governor of Louisiana in 1872-73 after Governor Henry Warmoth was impeached?
questions.explain: Pinckney B. S. Pinchback, Louisiana's lieutenant governor, served as governor for about five weeks after Governor Henry Warmoth was impeached.

questions.q: Secretary of State Seward survived a knife attack on April 14, 1865, partly because of what he was wearing?
options: A metal splint holding his broken jaw
A steel vest under his nightclothes
A heavy bandage over his chest
questions.explain: Seward had broken his jaw and arm in a carriage accident on April 5; the jaw splint helped deflect the attacker's blade.

questions.q: Booth's horse was held in the alley behind Ford's Theatre by which young employee, known as 'Peanuts'?
questions.explain: Stagehand Edman Spangler passed the horse to Joseph 'Peanuts' Burroughs; Hawk was on stage, Buckingham was the doorkeeper and Withers led the orchestra.

questions.q: Months before the assassination, who pulled Robert Todd Lincoln to safety when he slipped between a moving train and a platform in Jersey City?
questions.explain: The famous actor Edwin Booth, brother of John Wilkes Booth, rescued Robert Lincoln on a train platform, probably in 1864 or early 1865.

questions.q: John Wilkes Booth's father, an English-born actor famous for Shakespearean tragedy in the early 1800s, was who?
questions.explain: Junius Brutus Booth came to America in 1821 and became a leading tragedian; three of his sons, Junius Jr., Edwin and John Wilkes, became actors.

questions.q: In November 1864 the three Booth brothers acted together in New York to raise money for a Shakespeare statue in Central Park. Which play did they perform?
questions.explain: Edwin played Brutus, Junius Jr. played Cassius and John Wilkes played Mark Antony at the Winter Garden Theatre on November 25, 1864.

questions.q: While his parents were at Ford's Theatre on April 14, 1865, where was 12-year-old Tad Lincoln?
options: At a play at Grover's Theatre
At a church supper with his tutor
At the War Department telegraph office
questions.explain: Tad was watching Aladdin at Grover's Theatre a few blocks away when the manager announced that the president had been shot.

questions.q: The Lincoln conspirators were tried, and four were hanged, at the Washington Arsenal. What is that Army post called now?
questions.explain: The arsenal at Greenleaf Point, where the Anacostia meets the Potomac, was renamed for General Lesley McNair, killed in Normandy in 1944.

questions.q: Lincoln's 1865 funeral train to Springfield largely retraced the route of what earlier journey?
options: His 1861 trip to Washington as president-elect
His 1863 trip to dedicate the Gettysburg cemetery
His 1860 speaking tour after Cooper Union
His 1847 trip to take his seat in Congress
questions.explain: The funeral train ran about 1,600 miles through cities such as Philadelphia, New York, Cleveland and Chicago, much as his inaugural journey had.

questions.q: In February 1861, which detective arranged for President-elect Lincoln to pass secretly through Baltimore at night to foil a feared assassination plot?
questions.explain: Pinkerton, hired by a railroad president, uncovered the reported Baltimore Plot and moved Lincoln through the city ahead of schedule.

questions.q: Days after Lee's surrender in April 1865, Lincoln asked a band at the White House to play which song, joking that it was now a captured prize?
questions.explain: On April 10, 1865, Lincoln told a crowd that 'Dixie' was one of the best tunes he had ever heard and that the Union had fairly captured it.

questions.q: Julia Ward Howe wrote the words of 'The Battle Hymn of the Republic' in November 1861 while staying at which Washington hotel?
questions.explain: Howe wrote the poem at Willard's after seeing Union troops near Washington; the Atlantic Monthly printed it in February 1862.

questions.q: Which Union veteran, who had lost both legs in battle, took shorthand notes of witness statements in the Petersen House the night Lincoln was shot?
questions.explain: Corporal James Tanner, a War Department clerk, recorded testimony for Stanton; he later led the Pension Bureau and is buried at Arlington.

questions.q: As Booth leaped from the presidential box, his spur reportedly caught on a flag hung as decoration. What flag was it?
questions.explain: A flag of the Treasury Guard regiment hung on the box; Booth's spur snagged it and he landed hard on the stage, breaking his leg.

questions.q: Confederate spy Rose O'Neal Greenhow was held during the Civil War at which Washington prison, on the site of today's Supreme Court?
questions.explain: The Old Capitol, Congress's temporary home after 1814, became a Union prison for spies and political prisoners; the Supreme Court building rose there in the 1930s.

questions.q: Costly 1953 fighting for which hill, later the subject of a 1959 Gregory Peck film, came to symbolize battles fought while armistice talks dragged on?
questions.explain: U.S. troops fought for Pork Chop Hill in April and July 1953; Hamburger Hill and Hill 875 were Vietnam battles.

questions.q: The 65th Infantry Regiment, which fought in Korea and received the Congressional Gold Medal in 2014, was made up mostly of soldiers from where?
questions.explain: The 65th, nicknamed the Borinqueneers, was a largely Puerto Rican unit that fought in major Korean campaigns.

questions.q: Korea was the first war in which the U.S. military widely used what to carry wounded soldiers from the front to mobile surgical hospitals?
questions.explain: Helicopters such as the Bell H-13 flew wounded troops to MASH units, cutting the time before surgery and saving many lives.

questions.q: Which Boston Red Sox slugger flew 39 combat missions in Korea as a Marine pilot, sometimes as John Glenn's wingman?
questions.explain: Williams, recalled to the Marines in 1952, flew F9F Panther jets in Korea, then returned to baseball in 1953.

questions.q: Which country chaired the Neutral Nations Repatriation Commission and supplied troops to guard prisoners who refused to go home after the armistice?
questions.explain: Indian troops guarded the non-repatriated prisoners in the demilitarized zone in 1953-54 while each side tried to persuade them to return.

questions.q: Much of the western edge of the Pusan Perimeter in the summer of 1950 followed which river?
questions.explain: UN forces used the Naktong River as a natural barrier while holding the southeastern corner of Korea until the Inchon landing.

questions.q: Beginning in 1955, which Oregon couple's adoption of eight Korean children helped launch large-scale international adoption to the United States?
questions.explain: Congress passed a special bill so the Holts could adopt eight children; they then founded what became Holt International.

questions.q: U.S. 'special procurement' orders for trucks, uniforms and repairs during the Korean War boosted the recovery of which nearby former enemy nation?
questions.explain: Korean War orders gave Japanese industry a major boost and helped launch the country's rapid postwar growth.

questions.q: Which all-Black Army regiment, credited with retaking the town of Yechon in July 1950, was inactivated in 1951 as the Army integrated its units?
questions.explain: The 24th Infantry, a Black regiment since 1869, won an early victory at Yechon; it was inactivated in October 1951.

questions.q: Which 1950 law, passed after the North Korean invasion, let the president prioritize defense contracts and set controls on wages and prices?
questions.explain: The Defense Production Act of 1950 mobilized industry for Korea; the Internal Security Act of 1950 dealt with communist organizations instead.

questions.q: What was Operation Moolah during the Korean War?
options: A cash reward for any communist pilot who defected with a MiG-15
A program selling war bonds to Korean civilians
A secret fund to pay guerrillas behind North Korean lines
A plan to flood North Korea with counterfeit money
questions.explain: The U.S. offered $100,000 for a MiG-15; North Korean pilot No Kum-sok flew one to South Korea in September 1953, after the armistice.

questions.q: After Chinese forces entered the war, what did President Truman proclaim in December 1950?
options: A declaration of war on China
questions.explain: Proclamation 2914 declared a national emergency on December 16, 1950; the same day Truman created the Office of Defense Mobilization to speed rearmament.

questions.q: Which 1944 Supreme Court decision struck down the Texas Democratic Party's all-white primary election?
questions.explain: Smith v. Allwright held that the white primary violated the Fifteenth Amendment; Grovey v. Townsend (1935) had upheld it.

questions.q: Nine months before Rosa Parks's arrest, which 15-year-old was arrested for refusing to give up her seat on a Montgomery bus?
questions.explain: Colvin was arrested in March 1955 and later became a plaintiff in Browder v. Gayle, the case that ended Montgomery's bus segregation.

questions.q: During the Albany Movement of 1961-62 in Georgia, Police Chief Laurie Pritchett blunted the protests mainly by doing what?
options: Turning police dogs on the marchers
Calling in the Georgia National Guard
Granting the protesters' demands at once
Making mass arrests while avoiding public violence
questions.explain: Pritchett studied nonviolent tactics, jailed protesters in nearby counties and avoided brutal scenes, denying the movement national sympathy.

questions.q: Which Howard University law dean, Thurgood Marshall's mentor, designed the NAACP's legal campaign against segregated education?
questions.explain: Houston, called 'the man who killed Jim Crow,' trained a generation of Black lawyers and led NAACP cases in the 1930s.

questions.q: Which Arkansas NAACP president and newspaper publisher advised and supported the Little Rock Nine in 1957?
questions.explain: Daisy Bates and her husband published the Arkansas State Press; her home served as a base for the nine students.

questions.q: Norman Rockwell's painting The Problem We All Live With shows which six-year-old being escorted by U.S. marshals to a New Orleans school in 1960?
questions.explain: Ruby Bridges integrated William Frantz Elementary School in November 1960; Rockwell's painting appeared in Look magazine in 1964.

questions.q: Which 1947 federal appeals court decision ended the segregation of Mexican American children in Orange County, California, schools?
questions.explain: The Mendez ruling led California to repeal school segregation laws in 1947; Thurgood Marshall filed a brief in the case.

questions.q: In Hernandez v. Texas (1954), the Supreme Court ruled that the Fourteenth Amendment protected Mexican Americans against what?
questions.explain: The Court found that no Mexican American had served on a jury in Jackson County, Texas, in 25 years and overturned Pete Hernandez's conviction.

questions.q: King's first book, published in 1958, told the story of the Montgomery bus boycott. What was its title?
options: Where Do We Go from Here
questions.explain: Stride Toward Freedom: The Montgomery Story described the boycott and King's ideas on nonviolence.

questions.q: King was born in 1929 on Atlanta's Auburn Avenue, a thriving Black business and church district known by what nickname?
questions.explain: Sweet Auburn held Black-owned banks, insurance firms and Ebenezer Baptist Church; Bronzeville, Jackson Ward and Greenwood were in other cities.

questions.q: Gilbert Tennent's 1740 sermon The Danger of an Unconverted Ministry attacked whom?
options: Catholic priests serving in French Canada
Ministers who had never had a personal conversion experience
Quaker meetings that had no paid clergy
Deists who denied the Bible's miracles
questions.explain: Tennent, a New Light Presbyterian, said ministers without a felt conversion were unfit to preach, deepening Great Awakening splits.

questions.q: Revivalist Charles Grandison Finney seated people wrestling with conversion on a front pew called what?
questions.explain: The anxious bench was one of Finney's 'new measures,' along with protracted meetings and letting women pray aloud in mixed groups.

questions.q: Why did western New York earn the nickname 'burned-over district' in the early 1800s?
options: Forest fires had cleared much of its land for farms
Settlers had burned the towns of Seneca villages there
Canal boats brought frequent fires to its towns
Revivals swept it so often that few were left to convert
questions.explain: Waves of Second Great Awakening revivals, plus new movements such as Mormonism and Millerism, gave the region its name.

questions.q: The 1801 Cane Ridge camp meeting, which drew thousands to days of emotional preaching, took place in which state?
questions.explain: Cane Ridge, in Bourbon County, Kentucky, became a landmark of the Second Great Awakening on the frontier.

questions.q: Which religious community, led in America by Mother Ann Lee, practiced celibacy, shared property and worshiped with dancing?
questions.explain: The United Society of Believers in Christ's Second Appearing, called Shakers, grew to about 20 villages by the mid-1800s.

questions.q: Mormon founder Joseph Smith was killed by a mob in 1844 while held in a jail in which state?
questions.explain: Smith was killed at the jail in Carthage, Illinois; Brigham Young then led many Latter-day Saints west to the Great Salt Lake.

questions.q: Charles Sheldon's 1896 Social Gospel novel In His Steps popularized which question as a guide for daily life?
options: What must I do to be saved?
questions.explain: In His Steps, one of the best-selling novels of its era, urged Christians to apply Jesus's example to social problems.

questions.q: Which Chicago evangelist drew huge crowds to urban revivals in the 1870s with gospel singer Ira Sankey?
questions.explain: Moody and Sankey held revivals in Britain and American cities; Moody also founded what became the Moody Bible Institute.

questions.q: Which religious movement did Mary Baker Eddy found in 1879, teaching that prayer could heal illness?
questions.explain: Eddy set out her ideas in Science and Health (1875) and founded the Church of Christ, Scientist, in Boston in 1879.

questions.q: Congress passed the Religious Freedom Restoration Act of 1993 mainly in response to which Supreme Court ruling involving Native American peyote use?
questions.explain: Smith (1990) held that general laws need not exempt religious practice; RFRA required a compelling interest test instead.

questions.q: In Lee v. Weisman (1992), the Supreme Court ruled that public schools could not do what?
options: Let student religious clubs meet after school
Teach about world religions in history classes
Have clergy lead prayers at graduation ceremonies
Close for holidays such as Christmas
questions.explain: The Court held 5-4 that a rabbi's prayer at a Providence middle school graduation violated the Establishment Clause.

questions.q: Which anti-Catholic organization, founded in Iowa in 1887, tried to keep Catholics out of jobs and public office?
options: The Order of the Star-Spangled Banner
questions.explain: The APA peaked in the mid-1890s; the Know-Nothings and the Order of the Star-Spangled Banner were 1850s groups.

questions.q: Which short-lived agency of 1933-34 put about 4 million people to work during a single winter on roads, schools and parks?
questions.explain: The CWA, run by Harry Hopkins, hired workers quickly for the winter of 1933-34 and was shut down in the spring of 1934.

questions.q: Which 1933 New Deal agency gave federal grants to the states to fund relief for the unemployed?
questions.explain: FERA gave about $3 billion in grants for relief and work projects before the WPA took over much of its role in 1935.

questions.q: The Indian Reorganization Act of 1934, promoted by Commissioner John Collier, ended which earlier policy?
options: Removing eastern tribes west of the Mississippi
Paying tribes for lands taken by treaty
questions.explain: The 'Indian New Deal' halted allotment under the Dawes Act and encouraged tribes to adopt constitutions and self-government.

questions.q: The Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938 set the first federal minimum wage at what rate?
questions.explain: The act also limited the workweek, moving to 40 hours by 1940, and restricted child labor.

questions.q: In 1941 the Bonneville Power Administration hired which folk singer to write songs promoting dams on the Columbia River?
questions.explain: Guthrie wrote 26 songs in a month, including 'Roll On, Columbia' and 'Grand Coulee Dam.'

questions.q: Columbia professors Raymond Moley, Rexford Tugwell and Adolf Berle were part of FDR's circle of advisers known by what nickname?
questions.explain: The Brain Trust helped shape Roosevelt's 1932 campaign and early New Deal; the Kitchen Cabinet was Andrew Jackson's.

questions.q: The Civilian Conservation Corps, nicknamed 'Roosevelt's Tree Army,' enrolled mainly which group?
options: Young unmarried men from families on relief
Older farmers who had lost their land
Women whose husbands were out of work
Skilled craftsmen in the building trades
questions.explain: CCC enrollees lived in camps, sent most of their $30 monthly pay home and planted billions of trees.

questions.q: Who was the first chairman of the Securities and Exchange Commission, created in 1934?
questions.explain: Roosevelt picked Wall Street insider Joseph Kennedy, father of John F. Kennedy, to set up the new stock market regulator.

questions.q: Which song became Franklin Roosevelt's campaign theme in 1932 and a lasting Democratic anthem?
options: Brother, Can You Spare a Dime?
questions.explain: Played at the 1932 Democratic convention, 'Happy Days Are Here Again' became linked to Roosevelt and his party.

questions.q: As governor of New York in 1931, Roosevelt set up the Temporary Emergency Relief Administration, the first state agency of its kind. What did it do?
options: Insured savings deposits in state banks
Gave aid and work to unemployed New Yorkers
Bought surplus crops from upstate farmers
Built public power plants on state rivers
questions.explain: TERA, led by Harry Hopkins, was the first state relief agency of the Depression and a model for the New Deal.

questions.q: What was the main job of the Federal Housing Administration, created in 1934?
options: Building public housing for poor families
Insuring long-term mortgages made by private lenders
Setting rent limits in big cities
Lending money to build rural electric lines
questions.explain: FHA insurance made 20- to 30-year mortgages with small down payments common, though its rules also promoted redlining.

questions.q: Roosevelt's lifelong home in Hyde Park, New York, where he is buried in the rose garden, is called what?
questions.explain: Springwood overlooks the Hudson; Sagamore Hill was Theodore Roosevelt's home and Campobello was FDR's summer retreat.

questions.q: Which New Deal arts program, directed by Hallie Flanagan, was ended by Congress in 1939 amid charges of communist influence?
questions.explain: The Federal Theatre Project staged plays for millions; it was the only Federal One arts project Congress abolished outright, while the others continued under state sponsorship.

questions.q: Washington's only voyage outside mainland North America, in 1751, took him to which Caribbean island, where he survived smallpox?
questions.explain: Washington went with his ill half brother Lawrence; surviving smallpox there left him immune during the Revolution.

questions.q: Mount Vernon was named by Washington's half brother Lawrence in honor of whom?
options: A Virginia governor who granted the land
The family's ancestral village in England
A British admiral he had served under
A minister who had baptized the brothers
questions.explain: Lawrence Washington served under Admiral Edward Vernon in the 1741 attack on Cartagena and renamed the estate for him.

questions.q: Contrary to a popular legend, George Washington's false teeth were never made of what material?
questions.explain: His dentures used ivory, human and animal teeth, and metals such as lead; wood was not used.

questions.q: In 1797 Washington started what business at Mount Vernon, which soon became one of the largest of its kind in America?
questions.explain: By 1799 the distillery made about 11,000 gallons, run largely by enslaved workers.

questions.q: In the 1760s Washington shifted Mount Vernon's main cash crop from tobacco to what?
questions.explain: Tobacco wore out the soil and kept him in debt to British merchants; wheat could be milled into flour and sold locally.

questions.q: Why was the Washington Monument built a bit east and south of the spot where the White House and Capitol axes cross?
options: The ground at the planned site was too soft and marshy
A railroad depot already stood on the planned site
Congress wanted a clearer view from the Potomac
Robert Mills's design needed a natural hilltop
questions.explain: Builders moved the site to firmer ground; this is why the monument sits slightly off the Mall's main axes.

questions.q: A small granite marker near the Washington Monument shows the original crossing point of the White House and Capitol axes. What is it called?
questions.explain: The Jefferson Pier stone, replaced in 1889, marks where L'Enfant's axes cross; the Zero Milestone is a separate marker at the north edge of the Ellipse.

questions.q: Who served as the first president of the Washington National Monument Society, founded in 1833?
questions.explain: Marshall headed the society until his death in 1835; James Madison then took over the post.

questions.q: What Latin phrase, meaning 'Praise be to God,' is inscribed on the aluminum cap of the Washington Monument?
questions.explain: The phrase is on the east face of the cap set in December 1884; the other mottoes appear on the Great Seal.

questions.q: Horatio Greenough's 1840 statue of Washington, mocked for showing him bare-chested in a toga like Zeus, was moved out of which building?
questions.explain: The heavy statue was moved to the Capitol grounds in 1843 and to the Smithsonian in 1908; it is now at the National Museum of American History.

questions.q: Jefferson won a gold medal from a French agricultural society for designing an improved version of what farm tool?
questions.explain: Jefferson worked out a 'moldboard of least resistance' using mathematics so the plow turned soil with less effort.

questions.q: In Notes on the State of Virginia, Jefferson rebutted which French naturalist's claim that American animals were smaller and weaker than Europe's?
questions.explain: Jefferson listed the weights of American animals and later had a moose skeleton sent to Buffon in Paris.

questions.q: Which Army officer led an 1806-07 expedition into the Southwest during Jefferson's presidency and was arrested by Spanish authorities?
questions.explain: Pike explored the Arkansas River and Colorado, where Pikes Peak bears his name, before Spanish troops took him to Chihuahua.

questions.q: A 1998 DNA study, supported by later historical research, linked Thomas Jefferson to the children of which enslaved woman at Monticello?
questions.explain: Most historians, and Monticello, now accept that Jefferson fathered Sally Hemings's six children, four of whom survived.

questions.q: What did enslaved boys at Monticello produce in a workshop Jefferson set up in 1794 to bring in cash income?
questions.explain: Boys aged about 10 to 16 worked in the Monticello nailery, which sold nails to neighbors and builders.

questions.q: Jefferson described the growing United States, enlarged by the Louisiana Purchase, with what phrase?
questions.explain: Jefferson used 'empire of liberty' to describe a republic of farmers spreading across the continent.

questions.q: Jefferson called which three thinkers 'the three greatest men that have ever lived, without any exception'?
options: Francis Bacon, Isaac Newton and John Locke
John Locke, David Hume and Adam Smith
questions.explain: Jefferson kept portraits of Bacon, Newton and Locke at Monticello as his trinity of Enlightenment heroes.

questions.q: From 1797 to 1814 Jefferson was president of which Philadelphia learned society founded by Benjamin Franklin?
options: The American Academy of Arts and Sciences
questions.explain: Jefferson led the society while he was vice president and president, and used its members to plan the Lewis and Clark expedition.

questions.q: The Tidal Basin beside the Jefferson Memorial was created in the 1880s mainly for what purpose?
options: To store drinking water for the city
To hold ships waiting for the Navy Yard
To water the gardens on the Mall
To flush the Washington Channel with each tide
questions.explain: Gates let tidewater fill the basin and then released it to scour silt from the Washington Channel.

questions.q: Around 1801 Jefferson promoted which new medical practice by testing it on members of his household?
questions.explain: Jefferson oversaw vaccination of about 200 enslaved people, relatives and neighbors and later praised Edward Jenner in an 1806 letter.

questions.q: Jefferson wrote that which 1820 crisis 'like a fire bell in the night, awakened and filled me with terror'?
options: The panic and bank failures of 1819
The tariff dispute with South Carolina
The contested election of John Quincy Adams
The fight over admitting Missouri as a slave state
questions.explain: Jefferson feared that drawing a geographic line on slavery would one day split the Union.

questions.q: In early 1942 German U-boats sank many ships off the U.S. East Coast, helped at first by what?
options: Radar stations captured from the British
Ice fields that slowed escort ships
Coastal city lights that outlined ships at night
questions.explain: Until blackouts were enforced, glow from towns such as Miami and Atlantic City silhouetted tankers for U-boat crews.

questions.q: After U.S. and Filipino troops on the Bataan Peninsula surrendered in April 1942, thousands died during what?
options: The sinking of their rescue ships
A forced march to prison camps
questions.explain: On the Bataan Death March, tens of thousands of prisoners were forced to walk about 65 miles under brutal conditions.

questions.q: The Battle of the Coral Sea in May 1942 was the first naval battle in which what happened?
options: The opposing ships never sighted each other
A submarine sank an enemy battleship
Radar was used to find enemy ships
questions.explain: Carrier planes did all the fighting at Coral Sea, which halted Japan's move toward Port Moresby.

questions.q: The October 1944 Battle of Leyte Gulf, often called the largest naval battle in history, saw the first organized use of what Japanese tactic?
questions.explain: Japanese pilots deliberately crashed planes into U.S. ships at Leyte Gulf, a tactic used heavily at Okinawa.

questions.q: Which 1945 battle, the last major campaign of the Pacific war, was fought on an island in Japan's Ryukyu chain?
questions.explain: The Okinawa campaign lasted from April to June 1945 and cost more than 12,000 American lives and many more Japanese and Okinawan ones.

questions.q: Which federal agency, created in 1942, coordinated government news, posters and radio messages to build support for the war?
questions.explain: The OWI ran domestic and overseas propaganda; the Committee on Public Information had done similar work in World War I.

questions.q: In January 1944 the Allies landed at which Italian town, hoping to outflank German lines and speed the advance on Rome?
questions.explain: The Anzio beachhead was hemmed in for months; Allied troops finally entered Rome on June 4, 1944.

questions.q: U.S. troops suffered their first major defeat by German forces in February 1943 at which mountain pass in Tunisia?
questions.explain: Rommel's attack at Kasserine Pass exposed U.S. inexperience; George Patton took over II Corps soon afterward.

questions.q: In March 1945 U.S. troops seized an intact bridge across the Rhine River at which German town?
questions.explain: The capture of the Ludendorff Bridge at Remagen let Allied troops cross the Rhine before it collapsed ten days later.

questions.q: Most Japanese civilians first heard their emperor's voice on August 15, 1945, when he announced what by radio?
options: That Japan had declared war on the Soviet Union
That Japan would accept the Allied surrender terms
That Tokyo would be evacuated at once
That he would give up the throne
questions.explain: Hirohito's recorded broadcast told Japanese to 'endure the unendurable'; the formal surrender came September 2.

questions.q: Which Texas-born soldier, among the most decorated Americans of World War II and later a Hollywood actor, is buried at Arlington?
questions.explain: Murphy won the Medal of Honor in France in 1945 and starred in films such as To Hell and Back; his Arlington grave is among its most visited.

questions.q: At Tarawa in November 1943, many Marines were killed wading ashore because of what?
options: Minefields closed the only good beach
Low tides left landing craft stuck on coral reefs
Fog hid the beach from naval gunners
questions.explain: Higgins boats grounded on the reef, so Marines waded hundreds of yards under fire; amphibious tractors proved their worth.

questions.q: Capturing Saipan, Tinian and Guam in 1944 mattered to U.S. strategy mainly because these islands provided what?
options: Oil fields to fuel the Pacific Fleet
Bases for B-29 bombers within range of Japan
Harbors for an invasion of China
questions.explain: From the Marianas, B-29s bombed Japanese cities; the Enola Gay flew from Tinian in August 1945.

questions.q: In February 1943 four Army chaplains of different faiths gave their life jackets to others and went down with which torpedoed troop ship?
questions.explain: The Four Chaplains, two Protestants, a Catholic and a Jew, linked arms and prayed as the Dorchester sank off Greenland.

questions.q: The first campus antiwar 'teach-in,' an all-night session of lectures and debates in March 1965, took place at which university?
questions.explain: About 3,000 people attended the Ann Arbor teach-in, and the format spread to campuses across the country.

questions.q: In 1971 Vietnam Veterans Against the War held hearings in Detroit where veterans testified about atrocities. What were they called?
questions.explain: The name echoed Thomas Paine's 'summer soldier'; John Kerry later drew on the testimony before the Senate.

questions.q: On October 15, 1969, millions of Americans took part in which nationwide antiwar protest?
options: The Moratorium to End the War in Vietnam
questions.explain: Moratorium Day brought school walkouts, vigils and rallies; a larger march in Washington followed in November.

questions.q: The Case-Church Amendment of 1973 did what?
options: Repealed the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution
Barred further U.S. military action in Indochina without Congress's approval
questions.explain: The amendment, passed in June 1973, cut off funds for combat in Vietnam, Laos and Cambodia after August 15.

questions.q: Operation Babylift in April 1975 flew whom out of South Vietnam to the United States and other countries?
options: Thousands of orphaned and displaced children
questions.explain: About 3,000 children were airlifted; the first flight, a C-5A, crashed after takeoff, killing more than 130 people.

questions.q: The costly May 1969 assault on Ap Bia Mountain near the Laotian border became known by what nickname?
questions.explain: U.S. troops took the hill after ten days and then abandoned it, fueling criticism in Congress and the press.

questions.q: North Vietnam's large conventional invasion of South Vietnam in spring 1972 is known as what?
questions.explain: South Vietnamese forces, backed by U.S. air power in Operation Linebacker, stopped the offensive by the fall of 1972.

questions.q: The Agent Orange Act of 1991 helped Vietnam veterans by doing what?
options: Presuming that certain diseases were linked to herbicide exposure
Paying every veteran a one-time cash bonus
Banning herbicide spraying on U.S. farms
Paying for the Vietnam Veterans Memorial
questions.explain: The law let the VA treat listed illnesses as service-connected without each veteran proving exposure caused them.

questions.q: The black-and-white POW/MIA flag was designed in 1971 for which group?
options: The National League of POW/MIA Families
questions.explain: League member Mary Hoff, whose husband was missing, pushed for the flag; Congress recognized it in 1990.

questions.q: Journalist Ruben Salazar was killed during which August 1970 Los Angeles antiwar protest?
questions.explain: Chicano activists protested high Mexican American casualties in Vietnam; a sheriff's deputy's tear gas projectile killed Salazar.

questions.q: What role did James Parks, born enslaved on the Arlington estate, later have at the national cemetery?
options: He served as the first superintendent
He guarded the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier
He dug graves and worked there for decades
questions.explain: Parks worked at the cemetery for about 60 years and, when he died in 1929, was buried there by special permission.

questions.q: When Union troops occupied Arlington House in 1861, which enslaved housekeeper protected heirlooms that had belonged to George Washington?
questions.explain: Mary Custis Lee left the keys with Selina Gray, who reported soldiers' looting to General Irvin McDowell.

questions.q: Which heavyweight boxing champion, who served in the Army during World War II, was buried at Arlington in 1981?
questions.explain: President Reagan waived eligibility rules so Louis, champion from 1937 to 1949, could be buried at Arlington.

questions.q: Which son of Abraham Lincoln, a former secretary of war, is buried at Arlington rather than in the family tomb in Springfield?
questions.explain: Robert Todd Lincoln, war secretary under Garfield and Arthur, died in 1926; his widow chose Arlington.

questions.q: A memorial cairn at Arlington honors the 270 people killed in 1988 when a terrorist bomb destroyed which airliner over Lockerbie, Scotland?
questions.explain: The cairn is built of 270 Scottish stones, one for each victim; 189 of those killed were Americans.

questions.q: The Women in Military Service for America Memorial, dedicated in 1997, stands where?
options: In the courtyard of the Pentagon
At the ceremonial entrance to Arlington National Cemetery
questions.explain: The memorial was built into the semicircular Hemicycle wall at the cemetery's gateway, dating from the 1930s.

questions.q: Private Jacob Parrott became the first recipient of the Medal of Honor in 1863 for his part in which Civil War mission?
options: The sinking of the ironclad CSS Albemarle
The Andrews Raid to steal a Confederate locomotive
questions.explain: Union raiders seized the locomotive General in Georgia in 1862 to wreck a rail line; Parrott was later captured and beaten.

questions.q: Which Union veterans' organization, whose leader John A. Logan called for a national Decoration Day in 1868, became a force in Republican politics?
options: The Grand Army of the Republic
questions.explain: The GAR peaked at over 400,000 members around 1890 and lobbied hard for veterans' pensions.

questions.q: Arlington House, with its massive Greek Revival portico, was designed by which architect?
questions.explain: Hadfield, who also worked on the Capitol, designed the house for George Washington Parke Custis; it was finished in 1818.

questions.q: What role did Black Jack, a horse buried at Fort Myer beside Arlington, play in the funerals of Presidents Hoover, Kennedy and Johnson?
options: He pulled the caisson carrying the casket
He carried the officer leading the honor guard
He was the riderless horse in the procession
He led the mounted cavalry escort
questions.explain: The riderless horse, with boots reversed in the stirrups, symbolizes a fallen leader; Black Jack served in more than 1,000 funerals.

questions.q: Who selected the World War I Unknown Soldier in 1921 by placing white roses on one of four identical caskets?
questions.explain: Younger, a decorated soldier, made the choice at Chalons-sur-Marne; he is himself buried at Arlington.

questions.q: Which railroad, built by James J. Hill from Minnesota to Puget Sound, was finished in 1893 without federal land grants?
questions.explain: Hill's Great Northern reached Seattle in 1893 and survived that year's panic, when many land-grant lines went bankrupt.

questions.q: The Railroad Safety Appliance Act of 1893 required trains to have air brakes and what other device, to protect railroad workers?
questions.explain: Coupling cars by hand with links and pins had killed and maimed thousands of brakemen before the law took effect.

questions.q: Which city opened the first subway in the United States, in 1897?
questions.explain: Boston's Tremont Street Subway opened in 1897 to get streetcars off crowded streets; New York's first subway line opened in 1904.

questions.q: Outrage over the 1963 demolition of which New York landmark helped launch the modern historic preservation movement?
questions.explain: The loss of McKim, Mead and White's station led to New York's Landmarks Preservation Commission in 1965.

questions.q: During World War II, which slogan urged civilians to avoid crowding trains needed for troops and war freight?
options: Use it up, wear it out
Do with less so they'll have more
questions.explain: Railroads carried most wartime troop movements; government and railroad ads asked travelers to stay home.

questions.q: Which American-built locomotive began regular steam-powered passenger service in South Carolina on December 25, 1830?
questions.explain: The South Carolina Canal and Rail Road Company began service on December 25, 1830; the locomotive's boiler exploded the next year.

questions.q: Amtrak's Acela high-speed service, launched in 2000, runs on which route?
options: The Pacific Surfliner route in California
The Northeast Corridor between Boston and Washington
The line from Chicago to St. Louis
The route from Los Angeles to Las Vegas
questions.explain: Acela trains serve cities such as New York, Philadelphia and Baltimore, ending at Union Station in Washington.

questions.q: When the first segment of Washington's Metrorail opened in 1976, which line did it serve, with a stop at Union Station?
questions.explain: Service began on March 27, 1976, on a short Red Line stretch from Farragut North to Rhode Island Avenue.

questions.q: Smithsonian Secretary Samuel Langley's Aerodrome plunged into which river in two failed launches in late 1903?
questions.explain: Launched from a houseboat in October and December 1903, the Aerodrome crashed days before the Wrights flew at Kitty Hawk.

questions.q: Because of a dispute with the Smithsonian, where was the 1903 Wright Flyer exhibited from 1928 to 1948?
options: The Henry Ford Museum in Michigan
The Musee de l'Air in Paris
questions.explain: Orville Wright objected to the Smithsonian crediting Langley's Aerodrome; the Flyer came to Washington after the Smithsonian corrected its claims.

questions.q: Bessie Coleman, the first African American woman to earn a pilot's license, received it in 1921 in which country?
questions.explain: American flight schools turned her away, so Coleman learned French and trained in France; she became a stunt flier.

questions.q: The Wright brothers fought a long patent battle over aircraft control with which rival aviator and engine builder?
questions.explain: The suits over the Wrights' control system dragged on until World War I, when the government pushed a patent pool.

questions.q: Wernher von Braun, who later led design of the Saturn V rocket, came to the United States after World War II through which secret program?
questions.explain: Paperclip brought more than 1,600 German scientists and engineers to the U.S., despite many members' Nazi pasts.

questions.q: In June 1965, during Gemini 4, who became the first American to walk in space?
questions.explain: White spent about 20 minutes outside the capsule; he died in the Apollo 1 fire in 1967.

questions.q: In 1963, who became the first woman to travel into space?
questions.explain: The Soviet cosmonaut orbited Earth 48 times in Vostok 6; Sally Ride became the first American woman in space in 1983.

questions.q: In 1992, aboard the space shuttle Endeavour, who became the first African American woman in space?
questions.explain: Jemison, a physician and engineer, flew as a mission specialist on STS-47 in September 1992.

questions.q: In 1983, which Air Force pilot became the first African American to fly in space?
questions.explain: Bluford flew on Challenger's STS-8 mission in August 1983; McNair flew in 1984.

questions.q: The twin Voyager probes launched in 1977 each carry what, in case they are ever found by other beings?
options: A plaque listing every NASA astronaut by name
A sealed capsule of seeds from Earth's crops
A small sample of rock collected on the Moon
A gold-plated record of sounds and images from Earth
questions.explain: The Golden Record, assembled by a team led by Carl Sagan, holds greetings in 55 languages, music and natural sounds.

questions.q: Mars Pathfinder, which landed in 1997, carried the first wheeled rover to operate on Mars. What was it named?
questions.explain: Sojourner, named for Sojourner Truth, explored rocks near the landing site for about three months.

questions.q: Which wide-body airliner, nicknamed the 'jumbo jet,' entered passenger service with Pan Am in 1970?
questions.explain: The 747 carried far more passengers than earlier jets, lowering fares and opening long-distance travel to many more people.

questions.q: In 1933, who became the first pilot to fly solo around the world, in the Lockheed Vega Winnie Mae?
questions.explain: Post flew about 15,600 miles in under eight days; the Winnie Mae is in the National Air and Space Museum.

questions.q: A 1956 midair collision over the Grand Canyon that killed 128 people helped lead Congress to create which agency in 1958?
questions.explain: The Federal Aviation Act of 1958 gave one agency control of air traffic and safety; it became the Federal Aviation Administration in 1967.

questions.q: In 1962, federal marshals and troops enforced the enrollment of which Air Force veteran as the first Black student at the University of Mississippi?
questions.explain: Riots on the Oxford campus left two people dead before Meredith enrolled; he graduated in 1963.

questions.q: In February 1968, state highway patrolmen killed three Black students during a protest at South Carolina State College. What is the event called?
questions.explain: The students had protested a segregated bowling alley; the shooting drew far less national attention than Kent State two years later.

questions.q: In 1950, which diplomat became the first African American to win the Nobel Peace Prize, for mediating the 1949 Arab-Israeli armistice agreements?
questions.explain: Bunche, a UN official, also supported the civil rights movement and marched at Selma in 1965.

questions.q: In Alexander v. Holmes County Board of Education (1969), the Supreme Court ordered what?
options: Busing within a single city to balance schools
An immediate end to segregated school systems
Equal funding for Black and white schools
A ban on private segregated academies
questions.explain: The Court said 'all deliberate speed' was no longer acceptable and that districts must end dual systems at once.

questions.q: Which group, founded in 1853 by Ann Pamela Cunningham, bought Mount Vernon from the Washington family to preserve it?
options: The Daughters of the American Revolution
questions.explain: The association raised $200,000 and took over the estate in 1860; it still owns and runs Mount Vernon.

questions.q: Emanuel Leutze's famous 1851 painting Washington Crossing the Delaware was painted in which country?
questions.explain: Leutze, a German American artist, painted it in Dusseldorf; the large version hangs in the Metropolitan Museum of Art.

questions.q: As a teenager, Washington copied out a list of 110 maxims on manners and conduct. What are they called?
options: Rules of Civility and Decent Behaviour
questions.explain: The rules came from a French Jesuit guide of the 1590s; Washington copied them by about age 16.

questions.q: How many American flags fly in the circle around the base of the Washington Monument?
questions.explain: The ring of flags, one for each state, has numbered 50 since July 4, 1960, after Hawaii’s 1959 admission.

questions.q: The so-called Conway Cabal of 1777-78 was a reputed effort to do what?
options: Crown Washington king of the new nation
Replace Washington as commander with Horatio Gates
Move Congress from York back to Boston
questions.explain: After Gates's win at Saratoga, some officers and delegates criticized Washington; the scheme collapsed and General Thomas Conway resigned.

questions.q: On New Year's Day 1802, Baptists from Cheshire, Massachusetts, gave President Jefferson what gift to honor his support of religious liberty?
options: A Hebrew Bible bound in leather
A carved eagle for the White House
A wheel of cheese weighing more than 1,200 pounds
questions.explain: Elder John Leland delivered the 'Mammoth Cheese'; the same day Jefferson wrote his letter to the Danbury Baptists.

questions.q: Jefferson's 1779 Bill for the More General Diffusion of Knowledge proposed what for Virginia?
options: A state university for training clergy
A public library in every county
A system of free public schools
questions.explain: The bill would have given free elementary schooling to all free children; the legislature never fully passed it.

questions.q: Jefferson kept copies of his letters with a polygraph. What did this device do?
options: Made a copy with a second pen linked to his own
Measured a person's pulse to detect lies
Turned his letters into a secret cipher
Printed his letters with movable type
questions.explain: Jefferson used the polygraph, improved by Charles Willson Peale and John Isaac Hawkins, from 1804 on and called it the finest invention of the age.

questions.q: Which president announced the normalization of diplomatic relations with Vietnam in 1995?
questions.explain: Clinton had lifted the trade embargo in 1994; Vietnam veterans in the Senate such as John McCain and John Kerry backed the move.

questions.q: After 1975, many Vietnamese refugees settled in Westminster, California, building a business district known by what name?
questions.explain: Orange County's Little Saigon grew from the late 1970s into one of the largest Vietnamese communities outside Vietnam.

questions.q: In 1971 Senate testimony, which Vietnam veteran asked, 'How do you ask a man to be the last man to die for a mistake?'
questions.explain: Kerry spoke for Vietnam Veterans Against the War before the Foreign Relations Committee; he later served as senator and secretary of state.

questions.q: Operation Starlite in August 1965 is remembered as what?
options: The first major U.S. ground offensive of the war
The first U.S. bombing raid on Hanoi
The last evacuation of U.S. troops
The first use of Agent Orange
questions.explain: Marines attacked a Viet Cong regiment near Chu Lai, the first big U.S. ground battle against a main-force unit.

questions.q: Which paralyzed Marine veteran wrote the 1976 antiwar memoir Born on the Fourth of July?
questions.explain: Kovic, wounded in 1968, became an antiwar activist; Oliver Stone filmed his memoir in 1989.

questions.q: The Staggers Rail Act of 1980 helped revive struggling freight railroads by doing what?
options: Loosening federal control of rates and routes
questions.explain: Deregulation let railroads set rates and drop money-losing lines; freight railroads became profitable again in the following decades.

questions.q: In 1970, which railroad, formed by merging the Pennsylvania and New York Central lines, filed what was then the largest U.S. corporate bankruptcy?
questions.explain: Penn Central's collapse led Congress to create Amtrak for passengers and, in 1976, Conrail for northeastern freight.

questions.q: The 'Harvey Girls' were young women who worked where in the late 1800s and early 1900s?
options: In restaurants along the Santa Fe Railway
In textile mills in New England
questions.explain: Fred Harvey's restaurants and hotels fed rail travelers; thousands of young women moved west to work in them.

questions.q: Which New York station was saved from a planned office tower when the Supreme Court upheld the city's landmarks law in 1978?
questions.explain: In Penn Central Transportation Co. v. New York City, the Court ruled that landmark rules were not an unconstitutional taking.

questions.q: Electric 'interurban' railways, which boomed between about 1900 and 1915, mainly did what?
options: Carried coal from mines to seaports
Ran under city streets as subways
Linked cities with nearby towns and farm areas
questions.explain: Interurbans spread especially in the Midwest but faded as automobiles and paved roads spread in the 1920s.

questions.q: Which railroad engineer, killed in a 1900 wreck in Mississippi while trying to stop his train, became a folk hero in a popular ballad?
questions.explain: John Luther 'Casey' Jones stayed at the throttle of his Illinois Central train to slow it, saving his passengers.

questions.q: Bandleader Glenn Miller, honored with a memorial headstone at Arlington, disappeared in December 1944 while doing what?
options: Leading a USO tour in the Pacific
Flying across the English Channel to France
Sailing to North Africa with his band
Driving to the front in Belgium
questions.explain: Miller led the Army Air Forces band; his small plane vanished over the Channel and was never found.
